calls.head: The Golden Knights’ power play outclasses the Blackhawks’
calls.body: On the power play, Vegas is one of the league’s best and Chicago is one of the league’s worst. That’s about as far apart as two teams get.
calls.call: The Golden Knights’ power play creates more per 60 than the Blackhawks’.
calls.cite: Style fingerprint · this season blended with last · 0 and 0 games this season
calls.happened: On power-play expected goals per 60, Vegas had 7.8 per 60 and Chicago 3.7 per 60. Coming in, Vegas was at 8.7 per 60 and Chicago at 6.4 per 60.

calls.head: The Golden Knights roll four lines; the Blackhawks lean on their top six
calls.body: The Golden Knights are one of the league’s best for depth, at the deep end; the Blackhawks are one of the league’s worst, at the top-heavy end. Expect that gap to show.
calls.call: The Golden Knights spread their forward ice time deeper down the lineup than the Blackhawks.

calls.happened: On bottom-six share of forward ice time, Vegas had 43% and Chicago 43%. Coming in, Vegas was at 43% and Chicago at 40%.

VGK.head: We gave Vegas a 77% chance, and Vegas delivered.

CHI.head: We gave Chicago only a 23% chance, and it went the way we feared.

surprises.head: Chicago tried a different line
surprises.body: O. Moore, P. Kane, R. Kantserov played 9:03 together at 5-on-5, a trio that isn’t one of Chicago’s usual lines.

story.head: The Golden Knights beat the Blackhawks
paras: Victor Olofsson opened the scoring midway through the first. Five different Golden Knights scored.

The score was fair. Replay this game’s chances a hundred times and the Golden Knights win about seven in ten. By our Swing measure, Noah Hanifin had the best night of anyone. The Blackhawks tried a line they hadn’t used before: Oliver Moore, Patrick Kane and Roman Kantserov.

items.text: Whether the Blackhawks keep that line together in Utah on Thursday.
One of the preview’s two calls held.
